title: Like Pieces Bench
description: Push pieces of one size together or take some away, then tidy the answer before you write it down.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one small dot per phase at the footer's right (72-unit finger boxes, centred on the bubble), no text; in user AND AI mode each is a button (data-control phase-dot, data-phase k) that starts its phase

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Put pieces of one size together, or take some away, and then find out what still has to be done to the answer before it can be written down.
writeup.look: Two sets of equal pieces on a bench with their size written above it, a running count at the top left and a tidy rail along the foot.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Like Pieces Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the pieces standing on the bench against the pieces one whole takes, two numbers in ink arranged one above the other in the same way as the fraction being built, so the corner is read the same way round as the work. On the last phase it carries the stations the answer has been through and the stations it did not need. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The bench runs 1086 by 300 at 64,232, and the piece size is written once at 64,202, 420 by 40, and pinned there. Loose pieces lie on the bench, all of one size and one shape, separated, never overlapping and at most twenty to a heap. Push together slides the two heaps into one, piece by piece and not all at once, while the running count climbs and the pinned size does not move a hair; any attempt to edit the pinned size while a working is open is refused, and the stage prints that the pieces would have to be recut, which is a different sum. Lift away outlines the second fraction inside the heap and removes those pieces one at a time to a side ledge, where they stay drawn and countable rather than vanishing. Empty whole outlines stand behind the bench, 1086 by 150 at 64,382, each ruled into the pinned number of parts, so a heap that passes one whole visibly fills an outline and the green bracket spanning that outline closes over it. Gather the wholes lifts every full outline clear of the loose pieces and writes the mixed number underneath, whole part and proper fraction in their two places. The tidy rail runs along the foot, 1086 by 96 at 64,562, three labelled stations 340 by 96 reading gather the wholes, reduce, and nothing left to do. The answer walks the rail and each station reads it: a station the answer needs runs and writes its result, and a station it does not need is drawn greyed with its reason printed under it rather than skipped in silence. The tidied answer is always written BESIDE the untidied one and never over it, joined by a rose tie, because the first answer was not wrong and the tie says so. The crossword bay opens at 64,562 over the rail, 1086 by 150, a small interlocking grid whose every clue is a subtraction of two fractions of one size; each clue is carried to the bench, worked there and dropped into its cell. A cell whose subtraction leaves no pieces at all is drawn empty, stays empty, takes no fraction written into it, and is left out of the sorting step at the end that asks which of the filled cells share a lower number. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever an answer is asked for, with two extra keys that write the two places of a mixed number, and a small strip reading lowest terms, mixed number and nothing left to do, so a station can be named as well as run. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the parts a fraction counts are deep blue, the parts of that same whole which it leaves are amber, a whole shown entire or a bracket spanning one whole is green, a second writing of an amount already on the stage is rose, the greater of two fractions one of the chapter's rules can settle is vermilion, and a pair neither rule settles is sky blue, which is how this stage says undecided without saying wrong. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told from the rest by the drawn cut between them and by the label under it before it is ever told by a fill, and every cut, score line, cell edge and guide line is near-black. A fraction is drawn everywhere with its upper number above a level horizontal line and its lower number below, both upright and centred, and a mixed number is drawn as an upright whole number standing beside a stacked fraction. The pinned piece size is the one thing on this bench that no control can change while a working is open, including during a subtraction. Subtraction is exactly where the lower numbers start being taken apart, and a bench that allowed it there would teach the opposite of the rule it exists for.
writeup.finish: The card shows the workings the child built, each with its piece size written above it, and each answer in both its first and its tidied writing side by side.

phases.win: the heap count lands on the sum, the size above the bench has not moved, and the answer is written
phases.does: pushes the two sets together and reads the new count against the fixed size
phases.goal: adding like fractions adds the upper numbers and keeps the lower one
phases.says: Push them together and count. Did the pieces change size when you did?
phases.check: When you add two fractions that are both written in elevenths, why does the eleven stay as it is?
phases.feels: the count changes and the size written above the bench does not move at all
phases.hands: Cut two sheets into tenths and put three pieces in one heap and four in another, all of one size. Before they are pushed together, ask what is going to change and what is not. Push them into one heap, count it, and write the answer with the ten copied down from above rather than worked out.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what size is every piece on this bench? Second rung, the phase's: did pushing them together change that size? Third rung: the bench is cut to two heaps in quarters so the pushing and the counting can be done by eye. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: both fractions carry two numbers and the sum in front of them is an addition, so adding everything in sight is the move that looks complete.
wrong.move: adds the lower numbers as well as the upper ones, writing 3/10 and 4/10 as seven twentieths.
wrong.screen: the heaps are pushed together again at walking pace with the pinned ten lit above the bench, and the count climbs to seven while the size beside it holds. The seven over twenty the child wrote is then laid out on a second bench, where a whole one takes twenty pieces and seven of them fill barely a third of it, against a whole one in tenths with seven filled. Both benches stay drawn, side by side, and neither is marked.

wrong.why: reducing is a good move that has just been learnt, and a fraction in smaller numbers looks like a fraction that has been got ready.
wrong.move: tidies one of the two fractions before adding, reducing 2/12 to 1/6 and then trying to push it into a heap of twelfths.
wrong.screen: the push is refused with nothing marked, and the reason is drawn rather than stated: one piece from each heap is lifted out and laid side by side, and the sixth is plainly twice the size of the twelfth. The pinned size above the bench is lit and read out as the thing both heaps have to agree on. The child's reduced fraction stays on the ledge, the original heap of twelfths is laid back beside the other, and the push then goes through to ten twelfths.

phases.screen: two sets of pieces of one size with the size written above the bench
phases.soWhat: To add like fractions, add the upper numbers and keep the lower number, because the lower number says how big each piece is.
phases.concept: Adding the tops and nothing else

phases.win: the remaining pieces are counted, the size is unchanged and the difference is written
phases.does: lifts the marked pieces away and counts what is left
phases.goal: subtracting like fractions subtracts the upper numbers and keeps the lower one
phases.says: Take those pieces off. What is left, and what size are they?
phases.check: Find 7/13 less 2/13, and tell me what the thirteen in your answer is counting.
phases.feels: the pieces that left and the pieces that stayed are exactly the same size as each other
phases.hands: Put nine fourteenths in one heap. Outline four of them with a pencil, lift exactly those four away onto a side plate, and count what is left on the bench. Ask what size the pieces on the plate are, and what size the pieces still on the bench are.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many pieces did you lift away? Second rung, the phase's: how many are still on the bench, and what size are they? Third rung: the bench is cut to a heap in fifths with two lifted, so the counting can be done without the pad. Nothing lifted is ever put back for the child.

wrong.why: addition and subtraction have matched each other step for step all year, so whatever was done to the lower numbers in one is done to them in the other.
wrong.move: subtracts the lower numbers too, and cannot say what the answer is written over.
wrong.screen: the four pieces are lifted away again one at a time onto the ledge and the pinned fourteen stays lit above the bench throughout, with the pieces on the ledge and the pieces on the bench laid side by side and plainly the same size. The bench then asks for the answer to be laid out from the child's writing and there is no piece size to lay it in, so nothing can be built; the five pieces still on the bench are counted and written over the pinned number instead, and the child's writing stays beside it.

wrong.why: nine was the number this working began from and it is the number still printed on the question, so five out of the nine reads like a fair description of the bench.
wrong.move: counts the five pieces left and writes them over the nine the heap started with.
wrong.screen: the five remaining pieces are laid into an empty whole outline ruled into fourteen and they fill five of its fourteen places, with nine places left amber. Beside it an outline ruled into nine is drawn and the same five pieces will not fit its places at all, because a ninth is bigger than a fourteenth, and one of each is lifted out and laid together to show it. The child's answer stays in the slot and both outlines stay drawn.

phases.screen: one heap of pieces with a second fraction marked out inside it
phases.soWhat: To subtract like fractions, subtract the upper numbers and keep the lower number, which is the addition rule read backwards.
phases.concept: Taking away works the same way

phases.win: the whole ones stand apart from the loose pieces and the mixed number is written under them
phases.does: gathers the full whole aside and reads what is left beside it
phases.goal: an answer whose top is not smaller is written as a mixed number
phases.says: You have filled a whole one. Set it aside and say what is left over.
phases.check: Add 7/10 and 9/10 and write the answer as a mixed number. What did the ten do while you were tidying?
phases.feels: the pieces fill a whole one and the ones that did not fit are still lying there, still the same size
phases.hands: Give out eight ninths and seven ninths as two heaps of paper pieces, with an empty circle ruled into ninths lying behind them. Push the heaps together and fill the circle. When it closes, set it aside as one whole and ask what is still loose, then write the answer twice, once as a single fraction and once as a whole one with what is left beside it.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many pieces does one whole one take? Second rung, the phase's: how many whole ones did your heap fill, and how many pieces were over? Third rung: the bench is cut to a heap in thirds that passes one whole by one piece, so the gathering can be watched on four pieces. Nothing gathered is pushed back.

wrong.why: every step was right and the answer is a true fraction, and nothing in a written fraction says there is work still owed on it.
wrong.move: leaves the answer as fifteen ninths, because the adding was done correctly and the sum looks finished.
wrong.screen: the fifteen pieces are pushed into the outline behind the bench, it closes at the ninth and lifts clear as one whole with six pieces still loose under it. The fifteen ninths the child wrote stays on the stage and the rail writes the other readings beside it, joined by a rose tie rather than replacing it: one whole one and six ninths, and then five thirds and one whole one and two thirds once the reducing station has run. Nothing is crossed through.

wrong.why: fifteen was the number written a moment ago and it is still on the stage, so it looks like the number the six belongs over.
wrong.move: gathers the whole one and writes the leftover pieces over the count the heap had before gathering, giving one whole and six fifteenths.
wrong.screen: the six loose pieces are laid into a second outline ruled into ninths, where they fill six of its nine places, and the pinned nine is lit above the bench as the size every piece on it still is. An outline ruled into fifteen is drawn beside it and one of its places is laid against one loose piece, where the piece plainly overhangs. The child's writing stays on the stage with the tray's reading written under it.

phases.screen: a heap that has filled one whole outline with pieces still over
phases.soWhat: An answer whose upper number is not smaller than its lower one is written as a mixed number, and the lower number goes with it unchanged.
phases.concept: When the answer is more than one whole

phases.win: the tidied answer is written beside the untidied one, and a station that was not needed is shown skipped
phases.does: walks the answer along the rail, running only the steps it actually needs
phases.goal: an answer sharing a factor is reduced, and some answers are whole numbers
phases.says: Look at your answer once more. Is there anything left to do to it?
phases.check: Add 13/18 and 11/18, then tidy the answer as far as it will go and say which steps you used.
phases.feels: the sum was over some time ago and the answer still had one more thing owing on it
phases.hands: Work three subtractions on paper whose answers need different tidying: one that reduces, one that comes out a whole number and one that needs nothing done to it at all. Write each answer twice, as it first came out and as it finished, and write beside each one what was done to it or why nothing was.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: is the upper number of your answer smaller than the lower one? Second rung, the phase's: do those two numbers share anything above one? Third rung: the rail is cut to one station at a time with the other two greyed, so each question is asked on its own. Nothing already written is ever replaced.

wrong.why: the taking away was the question and the taking away is done, and a correct answer does not look like an answer with anything left owing on it.
wrong.move: writes six twelfths and stops, because the subtraction itself was finished.
wrong.screen: the answer walks the rail with the child's writing carried along beside it. The gathering station greys out with its reason printed, that the upper number is the smaller one so no whole is filled; the reducing station lights, because six and twelve share a factor above one, and it writes one half beside the six twelfths with a rose tie between them. Both writings stay on the stage and the six twelfths is never crossed through.

wrong.why: the tidying is a division and one division has been done, and the answer does now have smaller numbers in it.
wrong.move: reduces by dividing the upper number of the answer and leaving the lower number as it was.
wrong.screen: the reducing station draws both numbers lit together and refuses to write a rung on one of them, as the ladder did. The one twelfth the child built is laid out on a second bench, where a whole one takes twelve pieces and one of them fills a single place, against the six twelfths on the first bench filling six. Both benches stay drawn, and dividing both numbers by six is then run on a third, landing on one half with its single piece covering exactly the same length as the six.

phases.screen: the tidy rail with a written answer waiting at its first station
phases.soWhat: Look at every answer again before writing it down, because some need gathering, some need reducing, some need both, and some are already done.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the heap passes one whole. The pieces are pushed together one at a time and the empty outline behind the bench takes them in order, each piece dropping into its own ruled place, and at the ninth piece the outline closes: the green bracket spanning it comes round, the last cut line inside it fades to leave one unbroken circle, and the whole one lifts clear of the bench and stands apart while the six pieces that did not fit stay loose below it. Both readings write themselves at the same instant, fifteen ninths on one line and one whole one with six ninths beside it on the other, and the nine in each of them is drawn arriving from the pinned size at the top rather than from anywhere in the counting. Push the whole one back down and it opens into nine pieces again. Nothing else on the bench moves and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase two separate heaps of loose pieces lie on the bench, every piece in both of them the same size and shape, with that size written once above the bench and pinned there. On the second one heap stands alone with a second fraction marked out inside it by a drawn outline and nothing yet lifted. On the third a heap lies in front of a row of empty whole outlines, with more pieces in it than one outline will hold. On the fourth a written answer waits at the first station of the tidy rail with all three stations drawn and none of them run. The running count at the top left holds the pieces on the bench against the piece size pinned above it, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the gap between the two heaps, or the outline drawn inside the heap, or the first empty whole, or the answer sitting at the head of the rail, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks whether every piece here is the same size. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two like fractions at any piece size up to twenty, with the tidy rail live and the crossword bay open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on adding like fractions, subtracting them, writing an answer that passes one whole as a mixed number, and reducing what is left.
voiceLines: Two little heaps, and every piece in both of them is the same size.
Push them together and count. Did the pieces change size when you did?
Take those pieces off. What is left, and what size are they?
You have filled a whole one. Set it aside and say what is left over.
Look at your answer once more. Is there anything left to do to it?
Another pair. Check the piece size first, then count.
Free play. Any two like fractions at any piece size, the tidy rail live and the grid open.
Push them together again slowly, and keep looking at the size written above the bench.
Every answer counted and then looked at again, which is where most of the work was.

observations.why: Pushing pieces together makes more pieces and does not make them any bigger or any smaller.
observations.soWhat: Add the upper numbers and keep the lower number, because the lower number is the size of a piece.
observations.observe: The count above the bench climbed while the size written beside it never moved.

observations.why: The pieces are still all of one size, whether they are arriving or leaving.
observations.soWhat: Subtract the upper numbers and keep the lower number, which is the same rule read backwards.
observations.observe: Taking pieces away behaved exactly as putting them together had.

observations.why: Some answers need gathering, some need reducing, some need both and some need neither.
observations.soWhat: Look at every answer before tidying it, so that tidying is a decision and not a reflex.
observations.observe: The tidy rail greyed a station out and printed why, rather than quietly stepping over it.

observations.why: The pieces filled their wholes exactly, so nothing was standing loose to tidy.
observations.soWhat: An answer can be finished the moment it is written, and the rail says so out loud instead of leaving it looking unfinished.
observations.observe: One sum came out as a whole number with no fraction part left to reduce.

phases.screen: two sets of pieces of one size with the size written above the bench
phases.win: the heap count lands on the sum, the size above the bench has not moved, and the answer is written
phases.traceback: The heaps go back apart and are pushed together again piece by piece with the pinned size lit and the count climbing; the right fraction is written on the card.
ladder: What size is every piece on this bench?
Only the number of pieces grows when the heaps meet.
Is any piece bigger than another once the heaps have met?
Did pushing the heaps together change the size of a piece?
Count the pieces in the one heap, and keep the size pinned above them.

phases.screen: one heap of pieces with a second fraction marked out inside it
phases.win: the remaining pieces are counted, the size is unchanged and the difference is written
phases.traceback: The marked pieces are lifted to the ledge one at a time with the pinned size lit, the pieces left are counted, and the right fraction is written on the card.
ladder: How many pieces did you lift away?
Did lifting pieces off make the ones left any bigger?
Which bigger pieces cover the blue exactly, with none of them cut?
The lifted pieces are on the ledge, so how many stayed behind?
Count what is left on the bench, and keep the size pinned above it.

phases.screen: a heap that has filled one whole outline with pieces still over
phases.win: the whole ones stand apart from the loose pieces and the mixed number is written under them
phases.traceback: The pieces are pushed into the plates again one at a time, a full plate closes and lifts clear, and the lines that are not needed are rubbed out; the right answer is written on the card.
ladder: How many pieces does one whole plate take?
The whole is gathered, so what do the last two numbers share?
Did any piece spill onto a second plate?
How many full plates did your pieces make, and how many were left?
Count the full plates first, then the pieces on the last plate.

phases.screen: the tidy rail with a written answer waiting at its first station
phases.win: the tidied answer is written beside the untidied one, and a station that was not needed is shown skipped
phases.traceback: The sum is worked again on the plates; the rail runs the stations the answer needs, greys the others with the reason printed, and the right answer is written on the card.
ladder: Look at your answer again: is there one more thing to do to it?
Did the pieces fill more than one whole plate?
What is the biggest number that divides both of them?
Do the last two numbers share anything above one?
Each station of the rail asks one question about the answer.

items.win: Yes, pushing pieces together does not change their size.
Yes, 5 fourteenths are left, still fourteenths.
Yes, 5 thirteenths are left on the bench.
Yes, 5 twentieths cover the same part as 1 quarter.
Yes, 1 whole and 2 thirds, the same amount as 15 ninths.
Yes, 16 tenths gather and reduce to a mixed number.
Yes, 24 eighteenths gather and reduce all the way.
Yes, 4 twelfths of the tank is 1 third of it.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The heaps go back apart and are pushed together again piece by piece with the pinned size lit and the count climbing; the right fraction is written on the card.
Phase 2: The marked pieces are lifted to the ledge one at a time with the pinned size lit, the pieces left are counted, and the right fraction is written on the card.
Phase 3: The pieces are pushed into the plates again one at a time, a full plate closes and lifts clear, and the lines that are not needed are rubbed out; the right answer is written on the card.
Phase 4: The sum is worked again on the plates; the rail runs the stations the answer needs, greys the others with the reason printed, and the right answer is written on the card.

voice.opening: Two little heaps, and every piece in both of them is the same size.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Push, lift and tidy as many sums as you like.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: Every answer counted and then looked at again, which is where most of the work was.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

question.en: Add 3 tenths and 4 tenths, then write the sum on the card.
Now add 2 elevenths and 5 elevenths and write what they make.

items.planQuestion: When you add two fractions that are both written in elevenths, why does the eleven stay as it is?

question.en: When we add elevenths, why does the eleven stay the same?

items.planAnswer: Because the eleven says how big each piece is, and putting pieces together does not change their size

items.planQuestion: Find 11/20 less 6/20 and reduce the answer.

question.en: Find 11 twentieths less 6 twentieths and reduce the answer.

items.planQuestion: Add 8/9 and 7/9 and tidy the answer.

question.en: Add 8 ninths and 7 ninths and tidy the answer.

items.planQuestion: Add 7/10 and 9/10 and write the answer as a mixed number.

question.en: Add 7 tenths and 9 tenths and write the answer as a mixed number.

items.planAnswer: 16/10, which reduces to 8/5, and that is 1 3/5

items.planQuestion: Add 5/7 and 2/7 and say what the answer is worth.

question.en: Add 5 sevenths and 2 sevenths and say what the answer is worth.

items.planQuestion: Find 10/12 less 4/12 and reduce the answer.

question.en: Find 10 twelfths less 4 twelfths and reduce the answer.

items.planQuestion: Add 13/18 and 11/18, then tidy the answer as far as it will go.

question.en: Add 13 eighteenths and 11 eighteenths, then tidy it all the way.

items.planAnswer: 24/18, which reduces to 4/3, and that is 1 1/3

items.planQuestion: A tank is 7/12 full of water and 3/12 of the tank leaks away. What fraction of the tank still holds water, in lowest terms?

question.en: A tank has 12 equal parts, 7 full, 3 of them leak; what is left, lowest terms?

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted (the sound effects), speaking (always false: the lesson is silent), voice ("silent"), mascot, summaryRow, played, classroom, held (a classroom's parked piece of a long line), instruction (the pinned line), hint (the hint under it, or null), guideStep / guideSteps / guideOn (a guide-steps phase only), pieceSize, first, second, operation, tidied, complete

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files, on in every mode (the sound button switches them): correct, wrong (soft), win at a phase end, cheer at the last, a tick when a piece snaps, and cut, settle and trade where the picture moves

voiceLines.en: Two little heaps, and every piece in both of them is the same size.
Push them together and count. Did the pieces change size when you did?
Take those pieces off. What is left, and what size are they?
You have filled a whole one. Set it aside and say what is left over.
Look at your answer once more. Is there anything left to do to it?
Another pair. Check the piece size first, then count.
Free play. Any two like fractions at any piece size, the tidy rail live and the grid open.
Push them together again slowly, and keep looking at the size written above the bench.
Every answer counted and then looked at again, which is where most of the work was.
